summary: Single-author position paper arguing that coding agents now make mandatory human code review unnecessary: agents can serve every review goal (defects, style, security, knowledge transfer) more cheaply, AI-writes/human-reviews is a dead end because humans rubber-stamp and cannot scale, and the cost-benefit crossover 'has already been reached'. It proposes agent sign-off as a CI gate, with human approval kept for high-risk, novel-architecture and regulated changes, and rebuts five counter-arguments.

claims.claim: Every goal of code review can be served by agents at lower cost and higher throughput
claims.evidence: §IV-A cites prior work (Pornprasit & Tantithamthavorn [12], CodeReviewer [11]) and SWE-bench leaderboard trends (§III-A). No new data; SWE-bench measures issue resolution, not review; cited review studies show comparability on a fraction of cases, not superiority on all goals. Knowledge-transfer and team-awareness goals are asserted.

claims.claim: Human review of agent-generated code is illusory assurance (rubber-stamping) and does not scale
claims.evidence: §IV-B argues from a single cited study on reviewers' focus on surface issues [14] and throughput reasoning; no measurement of review effectiveness on agent PRs.

claims.claim: The crossover point where human review's marginal benefit no longer justifies its cost has already been reached
claims.evidence: §IV-C; asserted without any cost or defect-escape data. Also states agent reviews are 'deterministic', which is not generally true of LLM-based reviewers.

claims.claim: Prompt injection against reviewer agents is an unsolved, qualitatively new attack surface
claims.evidence: §VI-C concedes this with citation [32]; the paper offers no mitigation beyond treating it as a threat model, which undercuts the main thesis for adversarial contributions.

patterns.note: Agent reviewer as the default merge gate, with ensemble review and calibrated abstention proposed as mitigations; no evidence presented.
Argues against mandatory human approval, yet retains it for high-risk, architectural and regulated code paths (§V-A).
Developers become 'specifiers and orchestrators'; architecture coherence moved to design docs and ADRs.
Acknowledges reviewer-agent prompt injection as unsolved.
Structured, machine-readable review records (JSON/SARIF) and signed agent identities in VCS audit logs.

biases.detail: Uses SWE-bench resolution rates and competitive-programming rank as evidence for review capability.
'without precedent', 'dead end', 'eliminate it entirely', crossover 'already reached' with no data.
Cites studies favorable to LLM review; omits evidence on agent PR defects or reviewer-agent false negatives beyond brief counter-argument section.
Load-bearing claims are not tested; counter-arguments (§VI) are rebutted by assertion.

coi.affiliations: KTH Royal Institute of Technology (single author, Martin Monperrus)

verdict_reason: Provocative, well-structured position from an established SE researcher that is useful for framing merge-gate design, but its central claims are unsupported by new evidence and partly rely on mismatched metrics. Kept only as a labelled opinion; the deterministic gate will reject it on rigor <= 1, which is appropriate for evidence weighting.
applicability: For a Java backend team the paper's own carve-out applies: regulated content and code paths 'where a named human must bear legal accountability' keep human approval, so the team should not drop human review of ingestion logic that touches clinical or compliance-relevant content. The useful, transferable parts are: run an agent reviewer as a CI gate on every PR across all several repositories, emit SARIF/JSON so findings are host-neutral (works regardless of which agent host produced the change), give agent reviewers distinct signed identities, and move architectural coherence into specs/ADRs, which fits a spec-driven rollout. Treat reviewer-agent prompt injection as an open risk.

conflicts_with.detail: That study's organizing claim (from 3,100 coded practitioner documents) is that review is the control point through which a coding agent's effect on software is decided, the opposite of this paper's claim that review is obsolete.
Vision paper that keeps humans as supervisory operators of staged agentic review rather than removing review; partially compatible but rejects the 'end of review' framing.
